core_memory.user_crush: Someone I have a crush on
core_memory.user_crush_details: She is in my advanced algorithms class and we were on the same team for a project. I really got to know her during that time and found her to be funny and brilliant. She has a great sense of humor and keeps the mood light even in stressful situations.
core_memory.user_crush_family: I've been keeping my crush a secret from my family because I want to be certain about my feelings and where this might head before I open up to them. I don't want them to start planning a wedding prematurely, which has happened in my family before. I'll let them know when the time is right.
core_memory.user_crush_motivation: I'm worried about losing focus and getting distracted by romantic drama, but I think a bit of excitement or a spark could actually be motivational and give me an energy boost during these last two semesters. I need to find a balance between keeping to my schedule and allowing myself some excitement.
core_memory.user_crush_joke: I will wait until after our next group meeting and then ask her to grab coffee by cracking a joke about how we survived advanced algorithms together and now it's time to celebrate with a latte. I'm prepared for the possibility that she might say no, but I have a feeling she might just say yes.
core_memory.user_friends: I have formed really tight bonds with my friends at college, who have become like a second family to me. They make the stresses of being a CS major more manageable.

archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergrad research since my sophomore year, which has been an eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I was initially hesitant, but it turned out to be a great decision.
archival_memory.research_lab: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. We deal with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. My main task is working on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if needed.
archival_memory.student_life: I've seen the campus culture evolve over the years as a fourth-year Computer Science student. There are many ways to get involved beyond coding, and I've discovered different communities that make this place feel like a second home.
archival_memory.student_clubs: I joined the Computer Science Society, which hosts weekly meetups to discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and have industry speakers. It's a welcoming environment for beginners, and I can often get insights from fellow members who have worked on similar topics in internships.
archival_memory.vr_ar_club: I've been attending the VR/AR Club since my sophomore year, where I can share my passion for immersive analytics with like-minded people. The club is hands-on, with a VR lab in the engineering building where we host demos of each other's projects, from mini-games to experimental AR interfaces. It's inspiring to see the creativity and excitement among members, and it motivates me to push my own research further.
archival_memory.student_radio: I occasionally attend events at the student-run radio station, which hosts open-mic nights with singing, poetry readings, and stand-up comedy. I remember a friend from my Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set on stage, showcasing his soulful voice. It was a great reminder that there's more to people than their coding skills or group project roles.
archival_memory.campus_lawn: The central lawn is a popular spot on campus where students hang out between classes. Student organizations often set up booths there, offering freebies like stickers or candy to attract new members. I'm a sucker for free pizza, so if a club includes that in their ad, I'm usually tempted to join. The lawn is also where big campus events like Tech Fest take place. During Tech Fest, project teams showcase their prototypes, and recruiters look for innovative ideas. It's a big deal for engineering and CS students.
archival_memory.campus_culture: I believe campus culture is generally collaborative, with a sense of mutual support among students. While there are competitive elements, especially among seniors, the overall atmosphere encourages helping each other succeed. The campus hackathon was a defining experience for me. Thousands of students from diverse backgrounds came together for 24-36 hours, hacking away and learning from each other. It was chaotic but exhilarating. I formed a team with casual acquaintances, and the bond we formed during that all-nighter was incredible. Sharing experiences and challenges creates lasting friendships on campus.
archival_memory.dorm_life: I lived in a dorm specifically for engineering majors during my first two years. We affectionately called it "The Engi-House." Late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary, with some students working on assignments while others streamed e-sports tournaments. It could get intense, but it also meant that if you encountered a problem, there was always someone nearby who could offer help. We'd also have potlucks, watch Netflix together, or host a talent show to relax. It was a great way to build connections and have fun with fellow students.
archival_memory.volunteering: I volunteer at outreach events, such as the "Tech for Good" day where local high school students come to campus to learn programming and problem-solving. I help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's rewarding to see younger students light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage. I remember how I felt at that age, feeling overwhelmed by the tech world. By providing a positive first experience, I feel proud to be making a difference. These events showcase a different side of campus, highlighting the importance of community engagement and inspiring the next generation to pursue STEM fields.
archival_memory.social_scene: The social scene on campus is lively, with Greek life being one option for those interested. However, I found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people who share your interests. My friend joined the Robotics Team and found a second family there. We also have a close-knit group in the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk about tech when we're together; we also joke around, complain about cafeteria food, and plan weekend trips to the local hiking trails. It's a great way to build friendships beyond academics.
archival_memory.senior_week: I'm excited and a bit anxious for Senior Week, which is a series of events leading up to graduation. It includes a formal dance, a carnival, and a photo shoot in caps and gowns around iconic campus landmarks. My older friends who graduated last year said it was a bittersweet experience filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a sense of sadness that the journey's almost over. I've made so many memories here, and it's hard to believe it's almost time to leave. I'm looking forward to making the most of this final week as a student.
archival_memory.rivalry_game: The Rivalry Game is a big event on campus where our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college. Although I'm not a huge sports fan, I love the energy and excitement that week. People show their school spirit by wearing colors, painting their faces, and carrying banners. The night before the football game, we have a massive pep rally with fireworks, which is a real spectacle. Even if you don't attend the game, the campus vibe is electric. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer together. Whether we win or lose, it's a unifying moment for everyone on campus.
archival_memory.e_sports: Our school's e-sports team has gained official recognition, expanding the definition of campus sports. The e-sports arena is equipped with a wide seating area and a big screen for live streaming tournaments. It's not uncommon to see a hundred or more students gathering to cheer on our team during League of Legends or Overwatch matches. I'm glad to see e-sports becoming a legitimate campus institution, fostering a broader definition of competition and community.
archival_memory.midnight_breakfast: The Midnight Breakfast is a beloved tradition during finals week. It's a time for stressed-out students to come together and enjoy pancakes and cereal at midnight. Professors serve food, the school band performs, and everyone takes a collective break from studying. It's a small gesture, but it goes a long way in reminding us that we're not alone in feeling anxious about final exams. I appreciate how the campus culture prioritizes fun and camaraderie even during high-pressure times.
archival_memory.campus_life: I believe campus life is what you make of it. By exploring, approaching new people, and joining clubs, you can enrich your experience in countless ways. It's easy to get lost in your workload, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science. However, taking the time to attend events, volunteer, and connect with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. I'll remember the late-night coding, silly game nights in the dorm, Tech Fest presentations, hackathon adrenaline, and excited cheers at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. If you ever want a quick tour, I'd be happy to show you some of my favorite spots and introduce you to a few clubs. There's something for everyone here, and I'm glad I finally embraced all the campus has to offer.
archival_memory.user_future_plans: I'm in a similar situation. As a fourth-year Computer Science major, I'm feeling the pressure to have a solid plan for after graduation. I'm currently considering going into the industry for 5 years, but I haven't ruled out the possibility of attending grad school in the future.
archival_memory.user_job_market_goals: I'm aiming for software engineering roles that align with my passions for data visualization, VR/AR technologies, and data-driven product development. I'm drawn to companies that push boundaries in data analytics or immersive technologies, such as Unity, Unreal, or specialized VR startups. I'm considering both well-known tech giants and smaller companies where I can make a bigger impact earlier on.
archival_memory.user_job_search_process: I'm currently in the midst of campus recruiting, attending career fairs and submitting applications for software engineering and data engineering roles. I had a valuable internship last summer at a tech startup specializing in data analytics software for logistics companies. The experience taught me how a real development team operates and helped me build confidence in my skills. I believe this will make me stand out during interviews.
archival_memory.user_grad_school_considerations: I'm considering continuing my research in immersive analytics or human-computer interaction for large datasets through a graduate program. While I enjoy exploring topics in-depth, I also want to apply my knowledge in a commercial setting before committing to a PhD. Some peers suggest doing a part-time master's while working, while others recommend going all-in if I decide to pursue a graduate degree.
archival_memory.user_club_projects_influence: My involvement in campus clubs and projects has taught me the value of teamwork and problem-solving in high-stakes scenarios. I thrive in environments where I can collaborate with others, brainstorm solutions, and iterate until they work. I'm looking for a company that encourages cross-functional collaboration with designers, data scientists, product managers, and domain experts. The interdisciplinary vibe I've enjoyed in my research lab is something I want to continue in my professional life.
archival_memory.user_financial_considerations: Financial stability is important to me. I have student loans and want a stable income after graduation to pay them off quickly. A full-time engineering position offers a decent salary, which would help me achieve this. While I'm considering grad school, I'm aware that funding can be uncertain, and I want to have a secure financial foundation before making that commitment.
archival_memory.user_timeline_considerations: The timeline is important for me. I need to stay on top of company hiring waves and interview deadlines. I also set aside time each week to practice coding problems, brush up on coding patterns, and review data structures and algorithms. My advanced courses, such as Advanced Algorithms and Distributed Systems, have greatly boosted my confidence for technical interviews. I feel more comfortable discussing topics like concurrency, big-O notation, and architecture trade-offs.
archival_memory.user_company_reach_outs: I've received initial chats from a few companies, which is surreal. I'm trying to stay grounded and remember that it's just the beginning of the hiring process. I'm also exploring smaller companies or startups in my city or nearby tech hubs, as they often offer hands-on roles where you can learn from day one. The idea of joining a brand-new VR startup and building a product from scratch is very appealing to my entrepreneurial side.
archival_memory.user_entrepreneurial_aspirations: I've considered the idea of launching my own startup, possibly after gaining industry experience. I have a couple of ideas for VR-based training simulators or interactive data analytics platforms. Team up with talented friends from my advanced classes or the research lab, and we could potentially create a small venture. However, I'm aware of the challenges of maintaining a startup and the importance of financial independence. My parents have been supportive but also remind me to be realistic about living expenses.
archival_memory.user_family_and_location: I need to consider my family's location and how far I'm willing to move. While tech hubs like Silicon Valley, Seattle, and Austin are attractive, I also value being close to my family. Remote or hybrid roles could offer flexibility, allowing me to live near loved ones while still working for a big name or innovative startup. It's exciting to have so many options in the tech workforce, but it can be overwhelming to navigate them all.
archival_memory.user_growth_and_goals: I'm committed to continuous growth and avoiding stagnation in a rapidly evolving field. I'll consider a role successful if it offers opportunities for learning and skill development. My goal is to establish myself as a specialist in immersive tech for data. To achieve this, I'll stay curious, push my boundaries, and explore different paths. I'll finish out senior year strong, continue interviewing, and make a decision by late spring. I'm excited about the potential opportunities ahead and confident that I'll find the right fit.
archival_memory.user_friends: I have formed really tight bonds with my friends at college, who have become like a second family to me. They make the stresses of being a CS major more manageable.
archival_memory.user_roommate: My roommate and best friend from freshman year is Tony. We didn't know each other before that first semester, but we clicked right away over a conversation about a piece of software I was trying to prototype for an Intro to Programming class project. Tony's not even a CS major - he's in mechanical engineering - but we would bounce ideas off each other late into the night, and we realized we had more in common than we initially thought. We both love working with our hands, albeit in different ways: I love to code and design logic, while he loves building things physically. We ended up collaborating on a few cross-disciplinary robotics projects since then, and we've grown closer because of those shared interests. Tony's someone I can always call when I'm overwhelmed with an assignment or if I just want to grab a pizza after a long day.
archival_memory.user_sailing_friends: I met a couple of friends through the campus sailing club. It's a fun mix of personalities, and we treat sailing strategy like a puzzle. The camaraderie on the boat is unlike anything else I've experienced in other clubs. We meet at odd hours to catch the best conditions, so we really rely on each other to stay motivated. There's a deep mutual respect because we see each other's strengths and vulnerabilities in such a high-stakes environment. One friend, Mariah, has ended up becoming a close confidante for me. She encouraged me to apply for a more challenging research position in data science, telling me I should believe in my skills the way she believed in me. That's the kind of unwavering support we have for each other.
archival_memory.user_cs_friends: I've made plenty of connections through my computer science classes - study groups, group projects, or just the random folks I always saw in the lab at two in the morning, trying to debug code the night before a big assignment. There's this sense of solidarity that comes from those late-night coding sessions - like we're going through the trenches together. I vividly remember this one time in my sophomore year, there was a particularly infamously difficult systems programming course. Our final project was basically building a mini operating system kernel from scratch, and we were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's actually how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We ended up bonding over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?
archival_memory.user_gym_friends: I have some pretty good friends from the gym. Working out has always been an escape for me - I mentioned before that I love to blow off steam by lifting or doing cardio whenever I have a heavy workload. Over time, I kept seeing the same group of people in the early mornings, and it kind of turned into this friendly circle. One of those guys, Dean, is a fellow computer science major, but he's more into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. He and I started talking shop between sets, which led to us comparing notes on our classes, which then led to us being gym buddies who share nutritional tips, workout regimens - pretty much everything. Now, every so often, we'll game together, too. He's the one who got me hooked on a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's become a friendship built around mutual support - pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
archival_memory.user_gaming_friends: I have a circle of friends that's quite dear to me through gaming. I'm not a hardcore gamer, but I do spend a decent chunk of time on weekends playing multiplayer strategy games, especially when I need a mental break from writing code or reading research papers. We have this informal e-sports club that meets in a common lounge in our student center. I don't always go, but whenever I do, it's guaranteed quality time with friends. There's something special about gaming with a group in the same room - plenty of laughs, random inside jokes, that collective groan when a team fight goes south, and the ultimate hype when we pull off a last-second victory. I made a great friend, Derek, through that group - he's super skilled in networking security, and he taught me a bunch of techniques that later proved useful in a cybersecurity research project. And the best part is how naturally our friendship evolved - initially from a shared hobby, and later we just kept supporting each other academically.
archival_memory.user_library_friends: I have made friends in the campus library, which is a quieter space for me to study. As a fourth-year CS major, I have a loaded schedule, so the library is my go-to for a peaceful environment. Over the years, I've bumped into the same faces in the same corner desks. One of those people is Jackson, a law student who was reading case studies next to my stack of cryptography textbooks. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. Over time, we realized we shared an interest in debates - oddly enough, he loves analyzing political and ethical implications of new technologies, so I'd talk to him all day about algorithmic bias. We discovered that, even though we come from different disciplines, we both care about how technology intersects with society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.
archival_memory.user_everyday_friends: I've made great friends in unexpected, everyday-life situations, like in the dorm laundry room or while waiting in line for coffee. There was this one day when I was super stressed with a research deadline. I was up too late the night before, so I rushed to the campus cafe half-asleep, waiting in a long line. I started complaining - under my breath, but loud enough for the person behind me to hear - about how I needed more time for my research code to run. Turns out, she was also in the thick of her own mechanical engineering lab fiasco. We commiserated, shared a laugh, and ended up sitting together for coffee. That day, we bonded so much over academic stress that we exchanged contact info, and now, whenever we see each other on campus, we make a point to catch up. She might not be a 'best friend' in the sense of constant hangouts, but it's still a positive, supportive relationship that started organically.
archival_memory.user_unifying_factor: What unifies all these friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're all navigating this crazy journey together. Sometimes, people have this caricature of computer science majors as being antisocial or always stuck behind a screen, but truthfully, my experience has been the opposite. We form these deep connections, especially because the workload and pressure can be so high at times. We're in labs critiquing each other's code, or we're on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to some bug—and those challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.
archival_memory.user_graduation: As a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and that means a lot of goodbyes eventually. I'm excited about the future - internships, job prospects, maybe grad school. But I have to admit, I'm also dreading the day when all these friends I've made scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.
archival_memory.user_friendship_transcends_distance: I believe that real friendship is about having a strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I've learned that from Tony, who's interning across the country this semester, yet we still FaceTime regularly. I see the same dedication in others, like Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised that if either of us ends up in Europe, the other has to come visit.
archival_memory.user_gratitude: I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, random campus encounters - everything. They're truly an integral part of my college experience, and they remind me that there's more to this journey than racking up achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends... that's what success really looks like to me. And I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story - they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
